title: Decisions, calling and God's will
for: I need to make a big decision
subtitle: Eight short sessions for anyone at a fork in the road: what Scripture means by God's will, how Christians have discerned, calling, the fear of choosing wrong, closed doors, waiting, and a whole life offered.
intro: This track is for someone facing a choice that feels too big to get wrong: a job, a move, a person, a calling, the shape of the next ten years. It has eight sessions of about ten minutes. You can take them in a week if the decision is close, or slowly if it isn't. Each opens a page on this site, asks one question, gives you one thing to do and one verse to keep.

Every session starts where deciding actually hurts, goes underneath to the picture of God that makes it hurt, and ends somewhere Scripture and the long practice of the church can help. It won't tell you what to choose. It aims to make you the kind of person who can choose, and then live with it before God.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group, a class or a mentoring pair through Decisions, calling and God's will. The group is for adults at any stage: students choosing a path, people weighing a move or a marriage, people near retirement, people living with a choice they now regret. A leader doesn't need to have made every decision well. A leader needs to listen more than advise, and to refuse to tell anyone what God wants them to do.

Each person reads the session and opens its page before the group meets. The meeting doesn't repeat the teaching. It talks over what people found, using the group guide for that session, gathered below in order. The group is itself one of the means of guidance the track describes, so let it be a place of honest counsel.

sections.title: The group
body: Five to ten people is a good size, and a pair works well too, an older believer with a younger one. It helps when not everyone is facing a decision at once; people who have lived with a choice for twenty years have much to give people standing at the fork. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week, for eight meetings.

sections.title: The room
body: Make it plain at the first meeting that what is said stays in the room unless someone is in danger, and that anyone may pass on any question. Agree together that nobody in the group will claim to know what God wants another person to do. Counsel is offered as counsel, and the person deciding keeps the decision.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Five minutes: one person reads the verse aloud, and the passage around it when the session opens a chapter.
Thirty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order.
Ten minutes: how people got on with the last session's one thing to do, for anyone who wants to say.
Ten minutes: the prayer prompt, in your own words. Nobody has to pray aloud.
Five minutes: name the next session and the page it opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: Christians who honour Scripture hold different views of guidance: that God has a particular will for each life to be found, that his will is what he has revealed and the rest is wisdom, or that the Spirit still leads by impressions to be tested. Session two sets them out as their own holders would. The leader should do the same, without steering the group to one, and should say plainly that the creeds don't settle it.
When someone brings a real decision to the group, don't decide it for them. Ask questions that help them see, and know which pastor you would send them to for more.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: Decisions carry grief: a door that closed, a calling that never came, a choice that went badly and cannot be undone. When it comes, stop and listen, thank the person for trusting the group, and don't hand them a verse as an explanation. Speak with them on their own afterwards.

Some people cannot decide because anxiety or depression has taken hold of them, and some are being pressed toward a choice by someone who controls them. Take either seriously. Inability to decide that spreads to small things and comes with sleeplessness is worth a doctor's hearing, and no one should be told to pray harder instead.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when the weight is more than a group can carry: anxiety that will not let them sleep, despair after a loss of work or a closed door, regret that has turned into self-hatred, or any thought of not wanting to go on. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its pages on decisions, on fear of the future and on anxiety are good first doors. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor.

sessions.title: What God's will means in Scripture
teaching: When people ask what God's will is for their life, they usually mean something hidden: one right job, one right city, one right person, kept out of sight until they find it. Scripture uses the phrase in more than one way. Sometimes it means God's purposes, what he has decided shall happen, as when Paul speaks of the God “who works out everything by the counsel of His will” (Ephesians 1:11). That will is certain, and most of it is not shown in advance. “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever” (Deuteronomy 29:29).

More often the phrase means what God has already made plain. “For it is God’s will that you should be holy” (1 Thessalonians 4:3). He has told us to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly. And for the many choices Scripture doesn't name, he gives a third thing: the way of wisdom, promised to anyone who asks. Most of God's will is already revealed, and it is mostly about who you are becoming. That changes the question you bring to a decision.

open.label: What the Bible says about knowing God's will
open.why: The verses on God's will gathered, and why Scripture spends more breath on the person you become than on the next move.

also.label: Deuteronomy 29, passage by passage
also.why: The verse that divides the secret things of God from the things he has revealed, read where Moses said it.

also.label: Providence, in the Study Bible
also.why: What Scripture says about God's rule over all things, so that his purposes are not confused with a puzzle you must solve.

also.label: What Does the Bible Say About What I Am Facing?
also.why: Type the decision you are facing in your own words and see what Scripture says on it.

sessions.question: When you pray about a decision, are you asking God for information, or for wisdom?
sessions.do: Write the decision you are facing in one sentence. Under it, write three things you already know God wants of you, whichever way you choose.

verse.text: The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever, so that we may follow all the words of this law.

group.open: What were you taught, growing up or in church, about finding God's will?
discuss: What is the difference between God's purposes, which are mostly hidden, and his will that he has already made plain?
Why do you think we ask so often about the hidden things and so rarely about the revealed ones?
How would it change a decision you face if most of God's will is about who you become?
group.pray: Bring the decisions people in the group are facing to God, asking for wisdom, and thank him for what he has already made plain.

sessions.title: How Christians have discerned
teaching: The church has never had one method for decisions, but it has always used the same means. Scripture comes first, since nothing God leads you to will contradict what he has said. Then prayer, counsel, “Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed” (Proverbs 15:22), circumstances, and the church together. When the apostles met in Jerusalem they announced their decision with the words “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (Acts 15:28). In the sixteenth century Ignatius of Loyola taught believers to notice what draws them toward God and what drags them toward darkness and unrest.

Christians who honour Scripture hold three main views of how it works. Some hold that God has a particular will for each life, a dot on the map, and makes it known to those who seek it; they guard against a God consulted about morals and ignored about everything else. Some hold that his will is what he has revealed, and inside it a believer is free to choose wisely; they guard against superstition. Some stress the Spirit's present leading, tested against Scripture; they guard against a church that would be alarmed if God spoke. Each has a hard question to answer, and the creeds don't settle it.

open.label: Does God have a plan for my life?
open.why: The three views of guidance set out as their own holders would state them, with the strength and the hard question of each.

also.label: Acts 15, passage by passage
also.why: The first council of the church, and how the apostles reached a decision together before God.

also.label: The Counter-Reformation and the Wars of Religion
also.why: The church history lesson that tells how Ignatius of Loyola, a wounded soldier, came to found the Jesuits.

also.label: What the Bible says about hearing from God
also.why: How Scripture says God speaks, and why anything you think you hear is tested against what he has already said.

sessions.question: Which of the three views of guidance is closest to how you have actually made decisions?
sessions.do: Name two or three mature Christians who know you well. Ask one of them this week to hear your decision and to ask you questions about it, not to decide it for you.

verse.text: Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.

group.open: Who has given you the best advice you ever received, and how did they give it?
discuss: Which of the three views do you find most persuasive, and what is the strongest point of the one you find least persuasive?
The apostles said it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. What does it mean to decide together as a church?
Why is it dangerous when someone claims God has spoken in a way that ends the conversation?
group.pray: Ask God for wisdom for each decision in the room, and for the humility to take counsel and the courage to give it honestly.

sessions.title: Calling beyond a job
teaching: We have shrunk the word calling until it means a career, and a career that feels meaningful at that. So the student who doesn't know what to study, the retired man, the woman whose illness ended her work and the young father in a dull job all feel they have missed their calling. Scripture uses the word more widely. The first call is to Christ himself, and Paul's command is to “walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received” (Ephesians 4:1), which he spells out as humility, gentleness and patience, not a job title.

From that first call come others: to the people God has put near you, to a household, a church, a street, and to work of every kind. The Reformers fought to recover that, teaching that the farmer and the mother are as truly called as the monk. Paul told the Corinthians that “each one should lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him and to which God has called him” (1 Corinthians 7:17). You cannot miss your calling by choosing between two good jobs. You can only refuse to follow Christ in whichever you choose.

open.label: What the Bible says about calling and purpose
open.why: Why Scripture roots calling first in whose you are, and honours the ordinary work of hands and home.

also.label: Ephesians 4, passage by passage
also.why: Paul's charge to walk worthy of the calling, and what he says such a life looks like.

also.label: What does the Bible say about work and calling?
also.why: The long guide to work as worship, and to the difference between a calling and a career.

also.label: What's the point of my life?
also.why: For the person who feels everyone else got a calling and they got silence.

sessions.question: If your job were taken away tomorrow, what would remain of your calling?
sessions.do: List the people and places God has put you among right now: household, church, street, work. Beside each, write one way you could answer that call this week.

verse.text: As a prisoner in the Lord, then, I urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received:

group.open: What did you want to be when you were ten, and what happened to it?
discuss: Why do we use the word calling almost only for jobs, and who does that leave out?
Paul wrote about calling from prison. What does that say about where a calling can be lived?
How would it change a career decision to believe you cannot miss your calling by choosing between two good options?
group.pray: Give thanks for the people and places God has called each of you to now, and pray for anyone in the group whose work is uncertain.

sessions.title: Fear and anxiety about choosing wrong
teaching: Many people don't struggle to know what is wise. They struggle to choose at all. They make the list again, ask a fourth friend, wait for a sign, and the deadline passes and the choice is made for them. Underneath is usually fear: of regret, of blame, of a road that goes badly and is their fault. A picture of God makes it worse, the picture of one right answer hidden somewhere, so that every choice risks stepping outside his will for good. We also have more options than any generation before us, and more options means more ways to be wrong.

The Teacher of Ecclesiastes saw it long ago: “He who watches the wind will fail to sow, and he who observes the clouds will fail to reap” (Ecclesiastes 11:4). You do not know which seed will grow, so sow. Waiting for certainty is not the same as trusting God, and it can be a way of trying not to need him. Jesus said, “Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself” (Matthew 6:34). No choice you make in good faith will put you beyond his reach.

open.label: What the Bible says about indecision
open.why: Why indecision so often dresses as caution, and what Scripture offers the person frozen at the fork.

also.label: Ecclesiastes 11, passage by passage
also.why: The Teacher's word to the person waiting for perfect weather: you do not know which will succeed, so sow.

also.label: Is anxiety a spiritual failure?
also.why: For the reader whose indecision is part of a wider anxiety, and who has been told it is a lack of faith.

also.label: I'm scared about the future
also.why: For when fear of what is coming has become heavier than the decision itself, with places to turn.

sessions.question: What are you most afraid will happen if you choose wrong?
sessions.do: Write down the worst outcome you fear from each option. Then write beside each what God would still be to you if it happened. Set a date to decide, and tell someone the date.

verse.text: Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.

care: This passage is not a rebuke of people who live with an anxiety disorder, panic attacks or depression. Those are real illnesses of body and mind, and they need care, not blame. Getting help is not a lack of faith, and nothing in this verse forbids it. A doctor, a counselor, medicine, one trusted person who will stay can all be part of how God cares for you. The Honest Answer ‘Is my anxiety a spiritual failure?’ says more. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Are you someone who decides quickly or slowly, and how has that served you?
discuss: Why does the picture of one right answer make deciding so frightening?
The Teacher says whoever watches the wind will never sow. Where have you waited for certainty that never came?
How is trusting God different from waiting until you feel certain?
group.pray: Pray for anyone in the group who is frozen by a decision, and hand to God the outcomes no one here can control.

sessions.title: When a door closes
teaching: The job goes to someone else. The house sale falls through. The person says no. Many Christians read every closed door as God's message, and some read it as his verdict on them. Acts tells a more careful story. Paul and his companions were prevented by the Holy Spirit from speaking in the province of Asia, then tried to enter Bithynia, “but the Spirit of Jesus would not permit them” (Acts 16:7). Luke doesn't say how. Then came a vision of a man of Macedonia, and they went. The door that opened led to a beating and a prison cell in Philippi.

So a closed door isn't always punishment, and an open one isn't a promise of ease. Paul once had an open door in Troas and left it, because he had no peace while his friend Titus was missing. Doors matter; they are not a code. Some close through someone else's wrong, and that is a loss to grieve, not a sign to decode. “A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps” (Proverbs 16:9). The closed door is not the end of his leading.

open.label: Acts 16, passage by passage
open.why: Two closed roads, a vision in the night, and the open door that led to a prison and a jailer's baptism.

also.label: What the Bible says about disappointment
also.why: For the ache of a hope that did not happen, without hurrying past it to a lesson.

also.label: When the work is gone: unemployment and worth
also.why: The long guide for the door that closes hardest for many people, the loss of work, and what it does to a sense of worth.

also.label: Eight Weeks Toward a Decision You Can Live With
also.why: A slower road, a week at a time, for a decision that has been reopened by a door that shut.

sessions.question: Which closed door in your life are you still trying to read, and what if it was simply a loss?
sessions.do: Name one door that has closed on you. Tell God honestly what you hoped for behind it. Then ask what doors are open to you now that you have not looked at.

verse.text: A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps.

care: If your grief is heavy, please do not carry it alone. Tell someone you trust: a pastor, a friend, a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Is there a door that closed on you that you are now glad of?
discuss: Paul's open door led to prison. What does that say about reading circumstances as signs?
Why might Paul have walked away from an open door in Troas, and when might that be wise?
How do you tell the difference between a door God has closed and a loss you need to grieve?
group.pray: Pray for anyone in the group living with a closed door, naming the loss honestly, and ask God to show the doors that are open.

sessions.title: Waiting
teaching: Some decisions are not yours to make. You wait for the test result, the offer, the spouse who has not come, the child, the answer to a prayer you have prayed for years. Our age treats waiting as wasted time, something an app should remove. Scripture treats it as one of the main places faith is formed. Abraham was seventy-five when he left Haran and a hundred when Isaac was born. The psalmist waited “more than watchmen wait for the morning” (Psalm 130:6), which means through the whole dark, with no way to hurry the sun.

Waiting on God isn't passivity. It is doing the next faithful thing while the large thing stays out of your hands, and refusing to force an answer God hasn't given. It is also different from putting off a decision that is yours. “The LORD is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul who seeks Him” (Lamentations 3:25). The wait does not mean you are forgotten. Often it is where you learn that he was the thing you were waiting for.

open.label: How to Wait on God
open.why: What waiting on God looks like on an ordinary day, between the prayer and the answer that has not come.

also.label: Pray Psalm 130 slowly
also.why: The watchman's psalm, prayed a line at a time, for a night that feels long.

also.label: What do you do when God does not answer prayer?
also.why: The long guide to unanswered prayer and long waiting, with the saints who waited before us.

also.label: What the Bible says about waiting on God
also.why: The verses on waiting gathered, from Abraham to the prophets, and the strength promised to those who wait.

sessions.question: What are you waiting for, and what faithful thing could you do while you wait?
sessions.do: Pray Psalm 130 slowly once each day this week. Each day, do one ordinary faithful thing that the waiting has tempted you to neglect.

verse.text: The LORD is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul who seeks Him. It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD.

care: If ‘the depths’ describe your life now, and the night feels long, please do not carry it alone. The man who prayed this psalm was still waiting when it ended. Waiting is not a failure of faith. Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is the longest you have waited for something, and how did you live while you waited?
discuss: Abraham waited twenty-five years. What do you think the waiting did in him?
How do you tell waiting on God from avoiding a decision that is yours to make?
What helps you keep faith in a long wait, and what makes it harder?
group.pray: Name before God what each person is waiting for, and ask for strength to keep doing the next faithful thing.

sessions.title: Living with the choice you made
teaching: The decision is made, and now the second-guessing starts. The new job is harder than it looked, the move has left you lonely, the marriage, the degree, the house are not what you imagined. You run the other road in your head, where everything went well. Much of this comes from judging a choice by how it turned out, as if a hard result proves you missed God's will. Scripture has no picture of a single track you left at some forgotten junction. When the exiles in Babylon were living where they never chose to be, God told them, “Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat their produce” (Jeremiah 29:5).

Some past choices were wrong, and they call for repentance, which God gives freely. “Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret” (2 Corinthians 7:10). Others were wise and simply turned out hard; those you grieve, and need not confess. Ignatius counselled never to reverse a decision in a time of darkness and unrest. The place where you now stand is where God's will meets you today. He is not waiting back at the old fork.

open.label: What the Bible says about regret
open.why: The difference between the regret that leads to repentance and life and the regret that only circles the wound.

also.label: Jeremiah 29, passage by passage
also.why: The letter to exiles who did not choose Babylon, telling them to build, plant and seek the good of the city.

also.label: How to Examine Your Day (the Daily Examen)
also.why: A short evening practice for noticing where God met you in the life you actually have, not the one you imagine.

also.label: A guided study of Jeremiah 29
also.why: Seven steps through the exiles' letter, for reading it carefully and not only for its most quoted verse.

sessions.question: Is there a past choice you are still trying to undo in your head, and is it one to repent of or to grieve?
sessions.do: Write down one decision you keep second-guessing. Decide honestly whether it calls for repentance or for grief. Then name one way to build and plant where it has put you.

verse.text: Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf, for if it prospers, you too will prosper.”

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is a decision you made that turned out better than you feared, or worse than you hoped?
discuss: Why do we so often judge a decision by its outcome, and what does that assume about God?
What is the difference between a choice to repent of and a choice to grieve?
The exiles were told to build and plant in a place they never chose. Where is God asking you to do that?
group.pray: Bring the regrets in the room to God, asking forgiveness where it is needed and comfort where the loss is simply loss.

sessions.title: A whole life offered
teaching: Paul's most famous words about knowing God's will come after eleven chapters about mercy, and they begin with an offering, not a method. “Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans 12:1). Only then does he say that a renewed mind will be able to “test and approve what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2). Discernment is the fruit of a life already handed over. It is not a technique for getting an answer while the life stays your own.

That is the last thing this track leaves with you. The decision in front of you is real, and it deserves prayer, counsel and courage. But it is smaller than the question underneath it, which is whether the whole of you, the body, the hours, the plans, is on the altar. Jesus prayed in the garden, “Yet not My will, but Yours be done” (Luke 22:42), and walked toward a cross. A life offered like that can take either road. The next program, Explain It, turns to giving a reason for the hope such a life holds.

open.label: Romans 12, passage by passage
open.why: The living sacrifice and the renewed mind, read in the order Paul wrote them, and the life of love that follows.

also.label: What the Bible says about surrender
also.why: Why surrender in Scripture is the opening of a tired fist, not a defeat, and how Gethsemane gives it its truest picture.

also.label: Build a rule of life
also.why: A tool for shaping the ordinary rhythms of a week around a life offered to God, after the big decision is made.

also.label: Why we believe it: the reasons
also.why: The next track on the road, in Explain It: Why we believe it: the reasons. Take it up when this one has settled.

sessions.question: What part of your life are you still holding back while you ask God for direction?
sessions.do: Read Romans 12:1-2 aloud each morning this week. Before you make your decision, write one sentence offering the outcome to God, whichever way it goes.

verse.text: Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.

group.open: What is one decision you made during these eight weeks, large or small?
discuss: Why does Paul put the offering of the whole life before knowing God's will?
What would it mean to say Jesus' prayer in the garden about the decision you face?
Looking back over these sessions, what has changed in the way you think about God's will?
group.pray: Offer your lives to God together, each in your own words, and pray for each decision in the room to be made in that offering.
